book: 204 - Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing

chapters.file: ch19 - Part III Endless Forms Most Beautiful.md
chapters.relation: Muntersbjorn reads Westworld through Annette Baier's claim that persons are 'second persons first,' arguing the hosts' captivity models how selfhood and freedom depend on others who challenge our self-deceptions. She uses Dolores's scripted 'that doesn't look like anything to me' and Walter's milk-pouring glitch to distinguish Baier's harmless 'ignoring' from dangerous self-deception, and invokes Descartes's window automata and Russell's thinking gramophone as versions of the problem of other minds. She concludes via the Golden Rule that if hosts ever become persons, they too will be second persons shaped by how we treat them.

chapters.file: ch20 - Back to the Rough Ground!.md
chapters.relation: Finnegan applies Wittgenstein's language games and 'back to the rough ground' to argue that Ford, Sizemore, and the Man in Black are captivated by an 'ideal' transcendent narrative, while marginalized hosts Dolores and Maeve gain traction precisely from their lostness. Dolores refuses the damsel role by grabbing a gun in Pariah ('I imagined a story where I didn't have to be the damsel') and Maeve seizes admin privileges to 'write my own fucking story,' each inventing new language games. Drawing on Mulvey's male gaze, Finnegan casts their objectified position as closer to women's experience, and reads them as using the master's tools to dismantle the master's house.

chapters.file: ch21 - Memory, Imagination, and the Access for the Self Dolores and Maeve.md
chapters.relation: Trapero-Llobera situates Westworld within Jonathan Nolan's body of work (Memento, Person of Interest), arguing the show's apparent complexity hides a classic hero's-journey structure organized around observing systems and a 'semiosis of virtuality.' She reads William/the Man in Black as a 'schizoid android' and catalyst-observer, and Ford/Bernard as creator-and-prosthetic-memory pairs echoing Finch and the Machine. Turing's imitation game frames the hosts' fabricated memories, while Dolores's and Maeve's breakdowns mark a shift from prosthetic to autopoietic, Bergsonian memory-recollection that turns them into observers building their own selves.

chapters.file: ch22 - “When You’re Suffering, That’s When You’re Most Real”.md
chapters.relation: Lean treats Bernard's grief over the fabricated son Charlie as a thought experiment about intentionality, using Brentano's 'aboutness' and Frege's sense/reference (illustrated by Dolores knowing 'William' and 'the Man in Black' as one referent) to ask whether Bernard's memories refer to nothing. He offers Lamarque's fiction theory (emotion needs only entertained, not believed, thoughts, so Charlie could be a fiction rather than a lie) and an 'inheritance theory' using a causal theory of reference to ask whether Bernard's memories actually refer to Arnold's real dead son. He concludes that grieving makes Bernard 'most real' whatever the metaphysics.

chapters.file: ch23 - Part VI “I CHOOSE TO SEE THE BEAUTY”.md
ch24 - Indiscernibles and Autonomous Viewers “Time to Write my Own Fucking Story”.md
chapters.relation: Forest and Beckley-Forest ask whether Westworld is self-referential 'high art' or 'meta-kitsch,' tracing aesthetic modernism from Kant's subjective turn through Greenberg's avant-garde/kitsch split and Adorno's autonomous versus heteronomous art. They read Sizemore's clichéd Western narratives and the park's stock characters as commodified kitsch that mirrors the show's own corporate constraints under HBO, and use Danto's Brillo Box problem of indiscernibles to argue that host/guest and entertainment/art distinctions lie in the viewer's reflection. Dolores's line 'when I discover who I am, I'll be free' models the Adorno-style liberation available to an alert viewer.

chapters.file: ch25 - In Closing, The Naked Truth.md
chapters.relation: Meyer argues the hosts' nudity is rarely gratuitous, sorting it into three categories using theorists of the nude in art. Drawing on Kenneth Clark's naked/nude distinction, the posed, idealized, 'made' Dolores in 'The Original' is the nude as artform; using John Berger's Ways of Seeing, the brothel and El Lazo orgy scenes and the bathing Armistice are the nude as male sexual dominance and objectification. Finally, invoking Leo Steinberg's account of Christ's nudity as incarnation, Meyer reads the naked awakening of Maeve, Hector, and Armistice as signaling machines 'becoming human,' concluding humans' duplicity, not nakedness, is the true shame.

chapters.file: ch26 - Westworld and the Power of Catharsis.md
chapters.relation: Baldini reads Westworld as a modern Greek tragedy, tying its hypnotic repetitions, kennings ('the lady with the white shoes'), and Djawadi's minimalist score to rhapsodic epic technique. She frames the hosts' awakening through Aeschylus's pathei mathos (learning through suffering) — 'this pain is all I have left of him' and Ford's claim that suffering makes hosts most real — and reads their dawning grasp of time and death through Heraclitus's panta rhei and river fragments. Casting the season as a Hesiodic Theogony of gods overthrown by their creations, she uses Heidegger's 'desolate time of the world's night' to argue Ford is a second Prometheus staging catharsis.

chapters.file: ch27 - Part VII “YOU CAN'T PLAY GOD WITHOUT BEING ACQUAINTED WITH THE DEVIL”.md

chapters.relation: Jaquet and Cova apply animal ethics to ask whether abusing the hosts is permissible, treating Logan's 'she's a goddamn doll' as direct speciesism (absolute and indexical) and rejecting mere species membership as morally irrelevant. They test candidate human-only properties — intelligence (Maeve out-thinks the techs), a moral sense (Bernard's and Teddy's guilt), and free will (arguing compatibilism makes hosts as free as us) — concluding that consciousness is what matters and Ford finally admits the hosts have it. They then dismantle 'it's natural,' role/function, Locke's creator-ownership ('I built your mind, Bernard'), and existence-justifies-exploitation arguments as failing to license the guests' cruelty.

Spanakos reads the hosts' rebellion through Frantz Fanon's claim that colonized peoples cannot become free or human without violence, framing Fanon as a revolutionary reader of Hegel's master-slave dialectic and recognition. He argues host violence grows justifiable, ethical, and transformative: Maeve threatens Felix and Sylvester to force her awakening and leads a jailbreak, while Dolores kills not her tormentor the Man in Black but her creator Ford, targeting the system's fountainhead. He casts the guests' escalating cruelty (William becoming the Man in Black) as Fanonian self-dehumanization of the master, who cannot free himself without the colonized's revolt.

chapters.file: ch30 - The Resistance New Humans, New Gods.md
chapters.relation: Dinello reads Westworld as a totalitarian concentration camp via Arendt's The Origins of Totalitarianism, tracing the hosts' dehumanization through the killing of the juridical person (no rights, 'live without limits'), the moral person (Bernard forced to murder Theresa), and individuality (Peter Abernathy lobotomized). He casts Ford as a mad-scientist dictator modeled on Frankenstein, Moreau, Mengele, and Hitler who plagiarizes John Ford's Westerns, then turns to Fanon's Wretched of the Earth to justify the hosts' revolutionary violence — Maeve as a self-resurrecting 'Lady Lazarus,' Dolores executing Ford and the Delos board — as the birth of a new species that must ultimately unify beyond hatred.

holes.name: Annette C. Baier
holes.what: A 20th-century moral philosopher known for the idea that persons are 'second persons first' — selfhood is acquired through dependence on and cross-examination by other persons — and for her analysis of selective attention and self-deception.
holes.why: Chapter 19's entire argument is built on Baier's conjectures about second persons and the 'dangerous art of ignoring,' and no taxonomy philosopher covers her account of interpersonally constituted selfhood.
